newsitem.title: UK: Thousands stranded after UK "National" called off.
newsitem.headline: Thousands stranded after UK "National" called off.

text.p: A bomb alert blamed on the IRA forced the cancellation of Britain's best-known horse race, the Grand National steeplechase, and stranded thousands of racegoers overnight.

Race organisers, keen to show they were not cowed by the bomb threats, said they hoped to run Saturday's race on Monday if they could reach agreement with owners, trainers and other interested parties.
Police received two coded warning calls about bombs just 30 minutes before the Grand National, one of Britain's most popular sporting events, was due to start.
Security forcesd evacuated nearly 70,000 racegoers from the Aintree course near the northwestern city of Liverpool and carried out three controlled explosions on suspect packages but found no bombs.
They were unable to search the estimated 30,000 cars and coaches parked inside the course before nightfall, forcing their owners to spend the night in makeshift accommodation in Liverpool.
Some slept in sports halls and leisure centres, others put up in overcrowded hotels, while local radio stations received offers of help from local people prepared to give a bed to stranded racegoers.
No one laid immediate claim of responsibility for the Aintree alert, but Prime Minister John Major and other British political leaders condemned the Irish Republican Army for wrecking the race.
It appeared to be a further attempt by the IRA to bring the Northern Ireland issue to the forefront of the campaign for Britain's May 1 general election.

In pursuit of their campaign to end British rule in Northern Ireland, the guerrillas have in the last 10 days planted bombs on British railways and motorways and disrupted London's train services with hoax calls.

Major said the IRA's actions would set back Northern Ireland peace efforts. The guerrillas could not now declare a ceasefire and expect their political representatives be admitted to peace talks in the near future, he said.
Jockeys, trainers and owners were angry that one of the greatest days in Britsh racing had been ruined and they vowed to run the race as soon as possible.
A tearful Jenny Pitman, trainer of past winners Corbiere and Royal Athlete, called for the horses to be returned to the starting gate and the race to go ahead.
"We cannot be held to ransom and give in to these people. We have the lunatic element here. We can't give in to them," she said.
Jockey Carl Llewellyn, due to ride Camelot King in the big race, described the situation as sick. "Whoever did this are not sportsmen," he said.
Among those evacuated from Aintree was Queen Elizabeth's daughter, Princess Anne, who was ushered away from the course by detectives.

Security forces braced for further IRA dispruption. Middlesbrough play Leicester City in the soccer League Cup final at Wembley on Sunday, with the stadium expected to be filled to its 80,000 capacity.
